sessions.notes: This book was a struggle to read. I think there were too many details about who, what, where, etc. I did learn a lot about the history of computers in the 1950s and 1960s, though. In particular, I now have a appreciation for the timesharing revolution. I also built a lot of intuition around how deeply timeharing influenced UNIX's design.
Fond memories of walking around Paris reading this!

sessions.notes: The book has a "show, don't tell" problem but I enjoyed it quite a lot other than that. I was looking for a light, easy read after struggling with The Dream Machine for two months. This was exactly what I needed. I appreciate that it's not another "fate of the universe depends on us" story. I am sick of Hero's Journey stories. It's just interesting adventures in space.

I know a lot more about a contemporary theory of the origin of life.
But the book seemed to meander a lot. And it was full of A LOT of
technical detail. Arguably too much. The most valuable knowledge I
gained is a much deeper understanding and appreciation of ATP. The
author argues that it's even more fundamental than DNA and should
be considered a core symbol of life, right alongside the double helix.
